rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at moderate temperature to capture all 10 compounds and map the elution window without risking truncation. The wide range and midlength gradient should reveal whether the mixture is generally early, late, or spread across the run.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only gain is reducing analysis time. Shorten the gradient one step while keeping the same composition window and temperature to test how much faster we can go before any pair drops below full-credit resolution.

We are very close to the 10 min target with full resolution, and the limiting pair is still just above 1.5. Shortening tG by one more step is the most direct way to see if we can eliminate the remaining time penalty while preserving full-credit separation.

At 14 min the only issue is the critical 6/7 pair, while the last peak is already under 10 min. Lowering temperature one step should increase retention and often improve selectivity enough to recover that pair without giving up too much on run time.

The best region is clearly near the 16 min gradient, and temperature changes affect selectivity strongly. Test one step hotter at tG 16 to see whether the critical 6/7 pair improves enough to keep full resolution while pulling the last peak to 10 min or less.

Keep the successful 16 min, 40 C condition but reduce phi1 one step to make the effective gradient slightly shallower at the late end. This may recover margin for the critical mid-run pair while only modestly increasing the last peak time.

Since tG cannot be set between 14 and 16 min on this grid, probe a slightly narrower gradient window by raising phi0 one step while keeping the otherwise strong 16 min, 40 C method. This should compress the early region and may reduce the last peak time enough to improve CRF without sacrificing the already marginal critical pair.

The raise from phi0 0.05 to 0.10 improved both time and the critical pair, so continue one more step in the same direction while keeping tG and T fixed. This tests whether we can push the last peak to 10.00 min or below and reach the maximum CRF without losing full resolution.

You already have the maximum CRF, so this is a refinement experiment to see whether a shorter method can retain full resolution at the improved phi0. If it fails, injection 8 remains optimal; if it succeeds, it provides an equally optimal but faster method.

Since 0.15/0.95/16/40 already gives the maximum CRF, the only useful remaining question is whether the method can be shortened further in practice while preserving full resolution. Increasing phi0 one more step at the same tG and T will test the resolution margin of the critical pair under a slightly steeper effective gradient.

The best method has only a small resolution margin on the 6/7 pair, so test whether lowering phi1 one step can preserve or improve that margin while staying under 10 min. This maps robustness around the optimum without straying far from the proven maximum-CRF region.

With a perfect score already found, the remaining value is robustness mapping near the optimum. A one-step lower temperature at the best composition/gradient setting will show whether the method is temperature-sensitive around the critical 6/7 pair.

The temperature study shows 35 C harms selectivity badly, so test the opposite side one step above the optimum to bracket thermal robustness. This will confirm whether 40 C is a true local optimum and how sharply the critical pair deteriorates with heating.

Both temperature and phi0 studies indicate 40 C and phi0 0.15 are near-optimal, so now test a lower phi1 to probe the other side of the composition window. This checks whether a slightly shallower late gradient can maintain full resolution while still keeping the last peak under 10 min.

A perfect method is already in hand, so use remaining runs to quantify robustness around the optimum. Extending tG one step at the best phi0/phi1/T will show how much extra resolution margin is gained per time penalty and helps define the safe operating window.

This combines the two near-optimal alternatives that each gave full resolution with only a tiny time penalty, to probe a potentially broader robust region around the optimum. It may preserve the improved critical-pair margin from lower phi1 while recovering some speed from the lower phi0 setting.

The optimum is established, so this run extends the tG trend at the same best composition and temperature to complete the local response surface. It will confirm how resolution margin and last-peak time evolve on the slower side relative to the 16 and 18 min runs.

This fills the key missing point between the 14 min under-resolved run at phi0 0.05 and the perfect 16 min run at phi0 0.10/0.15. It tests whether raising phi0 can rescue the 14 min method enough to reach full resolution at an even shorter run time.

The mapping suggests phi0 controls the time/resolution tradeoff near the optimum, and this corner has not been tested. Running phi0 0.20 with phi1 0.90 at 16 min will define whether both window shifts together over-compress the critical pair or reveal another robust high-speed region.

Now that a second perfect point is found at phi0 0.20/phi1 0.90/16/40, the next informative test is whether this shifted window tolerates a shorter gradient better than the original optimum. A 14 min run will show whether full resolution can be retained in an even faster practical method.

The second perfect plateau at phi0 0.20/phi1 0.90 suggests the optimum may extend to slightly stronger starting conditions. Testing phi0 0.25 at the same phi1, tG, and T will define the upper edge of that plateau and the tolerance of the critical 6/7 pair.

The upper phi0 edge has been found, so use a remaining run to map the lower phi1 edge around the second perfect point. This will show whether the 0.20/0.90/16/40 optimum is robust to a slightly shallower late gradient or if phi1 0.90 is already near the limit.

With the optimum already secured, use the last few runs to understand whether temperature can rescue a fast 14 min method near the stronger-window settings. Testing 0.20/0.95/14 at 35 C specifically probes whether the 6/7 pair can be improved without sacrificing the already short t_last.

The 35 C test showed cooling a fast 14 min method causes a severe 5/6 selectivity collapse, so bracket the other side with 45 C at the same composition. This final thermal comparison will complete the picture of how temperature perturbs the fast method near the optimum region.

Use the final run to complete the boundary map near the stronger-window region by testing whether lowering phi1 can offset the excessive compression seen at phi0 0.25. This defines whether the failure at phi0 0.25 is mainly due to too-strong starting conditions alone or the combined window shape.
